We characterize a natural class of modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension as representation categories of twisted doubles of finite p-groups. We also show that a nilpotent braided fusion category C admits an analogue of the Sylow decomposition. If the simple objects of C have integral Frobenius-Perron dimensions then C is group-theoretical. As a consequence, we obtain that semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension are group-theoretical. Our arguments are based on a reconstruction of twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories (this is reminiscent to the characterization of doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras in terms of Manin pairs).

outputs.L1: We characterize a natural class of modular categories of prime-power Frobenius–Perron dimension as representation categories of twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups. We also show that a nilpotent braided fusion category \(\mathcal{C}\) admits an analogue of the Sylow decomposition. If the simple objects of \(\mathcal{C}\) have integral Frobenius–Perron dimensions, then \(\mathcal{C}\) is group-theoretical. Consequently, semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime-power dimension are group-theoretical. Our arguments rely on reconstructing twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories, an approach reminiscent of the characterization of doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras in terms of Manin pairs.
outputs.L2: We identify a broad family of modular categories whose Frobenius–Perron dimensions are prime powers, proving that they arise as representation categories of twisted doubles associated with finite \(p\)-groups. We further establish a Sylow-type factorization for any nilpotent braided fusion category \(\mathcal C\). When every simple object of \(\mathcal C\) has integral Frobenius–Perron dimension, the category is group-theoretical. It follows in particular that all semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime-power dimension are group-theoretical. The proofs rely on recovering twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories inside modular categories, paralleling the description of doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras through Manin pairs.
outputs.L3:
A natural class of modular categories of prime-power Frobenius–Perron dimension can be characterized in group-theoretical terms: such categories arise as representation categories of twisted Drinfeld doubles of finite \(p\)-groups. More precisely, the relevant modular categories are equivalent to categories of representations of \(D^{\omega}(G)\), where \(G\) is a finite \(p\)-group and \(\omega\) is a \(3\)-cocycle encoding the associativity twist.

A central ingredient in this characterization is a categorical analogue of the classical Sylow decomposition. Nilpotent braided fusion categories decompose into braided fusion subcategories whose Frobenius–Perron dimensions are powers of distinct primes. These prime-power components play the role of Sylow subgroups and allow structural questions about a nilpotent category to be reduced to the corresponding questions for its individual prime components.

This decomposition also leads to a strong group-theoreticality result. If a nilpotent braided fusion category has integral Frobenius–Perron dimensions for all of its simple objects, then it is group-theoretical: it is Morita equivalent to a pointed fusion category. As a consequence, semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime-power dimension are group-theoretical, so their representation categories can ultimately be described using finite groups and cohomological twisting data.

The underlying arguments proceed by identifying and analyzing Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories. From such a subcategory, one can reconstruct a finite group together with an appropriate \(3\)-cocycle and thereby recover the modular category as the representation category of a twisted group double. This reconstruction is closely analogous to the classical description of doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras in terms of Manin pairs: in both settings, a distinguished maximal isotropic structure provides the data needed to recover the corresponding double.
outputs.L4:
The work studies braided fusion categories whose Frobenius–Perron dimension is a power of a prime. Its principal tool is a reconstruction theorem based on Lagrangian subcategories: when a modular category contains such a subcategory, it can be recovered as the representation category of a twisted quantum double \(D^{\omega}(G)\), where \(G\) is a finite group and \(\omega\in Z^{3}(G,k^{\times})\) determines the twisting. In the prime-power setting, the reconstructed group may be chosen to be a finite \(p\)-group. This gives a concrete description of the relevant modular categories in terms of finite-group and cohomological data.

The paper also establishes a Sylow-type theory for nilpotent braided fusion categories. Analogously to the decomposition of a finite nilpotent group into its Sylow subgroups, a nilpotent braided fusion category decomposes into a Deligne tensor product of braided fusion categories of prime-power Frobenius–Perron dimension. This reduces many structural questions about nilpotent braided categories to the corresponding questions for their prime-power components.

As a central application, the work proves that modular categories of prime-power Frobenius–Perron dimension whose simple objects all have integral Frobenius–Perron dimensions are group-theoretical. Thus they are Morita equivalent to pointed fusion categories and can be described through finite groups, cocycles, and twisted doubles. The same methods yield an algebraic consequence: every semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra of prime-power dimension has a group-theoretical representation category. These results extend the categorical analogies with finite \(p\)-groups and show that integrality, modularity, and prime-power dimension impose strong group-theoretical constraints.
outputs.L5:
Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, Oskar Perron, and Ludwig Sylow made foundational contributions to modern algebra.

The **Perron–Frobenius theorem**, named after Perron and Frobenius, concerns matrices with nonnegative entries. It states, under suitable conditions, that such a matrix has a dominant real eigenvalue with a corresponding nonnegative eigenvector. This result is essential in probability, economics, graph theory, dynamical systems, and the study of Markov chains.

In group theory, the **Sylow theorems** describe the subgroups of a finite group whose orders are powers of a prime. If a prime power \(p^k\) divides the order of a finite group, then the group contains a subgroup of order \(p^k\). The theorems also explain how these Sylow subgroups are related by conjugation and restrict how many of them can exist.

Frobenius helped connect these areas to the broader development of representation theory. By representing group elements as matrices, abstract questions about finite groups—including their Sylow subgroups—can be investigated using linear algebra and character theory. Thus, the names Frobenius, Perron, and Sylow reflect two closely connected traditions: the structural study of groups and the analysis of matrices and their eigenvalues.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on modular categories of prime-power Frobenius–Perron dimension, Sylow decompositions for nilpotent braided fusion categories, and group-theoretical quasi-Hopf algebras.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate braided fusion categories through analogues of Sylow theory and applications to modular categories and quasi-Hopf algebras. We establish a Sylow decomposition for nilpotent braided fusion categories, showing that such a category factors canonically, up to braided equivalence, as a Deligne tensor product of braided fusion categories of prime-power Frobenius–Perron dimension. This reduces structural and classification questions to the prime-power case. We then study modular categories of Frobenius–Perron dimension \(p^n\), deriving constraints on their invertible objects, fusion subcategories, and centralizers, and identifying conditions under which they are pointed or group-theoretical. As an application, we obtain corresponding decomposition and recognition results for finite-dimensional semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras whose representation categories are nilpotent and braided. In particular, the categorical Sylow factors yield prime-power components at the level of gauge-equivalence classes and clarify when the resulting quasi-Hopf algebras arise from group-theoretical data. These results provide a unified framework for analyzing nilpotent modular categories and group-theoretical quasi-Hopf algebras via their local prime-power constituents.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a paper characterizing modular categories as representation categories of twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s central result is an intrinsic recognition theorem for twisted quantum doubles.

- For a finite group \(G\) and \(3\)-cocycle \(\omega\in Z^{3}(G,k^\times)\),
  \[
  \operatorname{Rep}(D^\omega(G))\simeq \mathcal Z(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega),
  \]
  where \(\mathcal Z\) denotes the Drinfeld center.

- A modular category \(\mathcal C\) is braided equivalent to \(\operatorname{Rep}(D^\omega(G))\) for some finite \(G\) **if and only if** \(\mathcal C\) contains a **Lagrangian subcategory**. This is a Tannakian subcategory
  \[
  \mathcal L\simeq \operatorname{Rep}(G)
  \]
  satisfying \(\mathcal L=\mathcal L'\), its own Müger centralizer. Equivalently,
  \[
  \operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal L)^2=\operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C).
  \]

- In the \(p\)-group case, if
  \[
  \operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C)=p^{2n},
  \]
  then the reconstructed group has order \(p^n\), hence is a finite \(p\)-group. Thus twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups are precisely the modular categories of \(p\)-power dimension possessing such a Lagrangian/Tannakian subcategory. Merely having \(p\)-power or square dimension is not enough.

- The proof reconstructs the pointed fusion category \(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega\) from the Lagrangian subcategory, showing
  \[
  \mathcal C\simeq \mathcal Z(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega).
  \]

- The paper also describes Lagrangian subcategories of a given \(\operatorname{Rep}(D^\omega(G))\) in group-cohomological terms, using suitable normal abelian subgroups and compatible invariant bicharacter data.

A key consequence is that braided equivalences between twisted-double categories are governed by categorical Morita equivalences between the underlying pointed categories \(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega\). The result therefore turns the problem of recognizing these modular categories into the concrete task of finding a maximal isotropic—or Lagrangian—Tannakian sector.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise mathematical abstract explaining how Lagrangian subcategories can be used to reconstruct twisted group doubles and derive consequences for integral nilpotent braided fusion categories.
counterfactuals.output:
We show that a nondegenerate braided fusion category \(\mathcal C\) containing a Lagrangian subcategory \(\mathcal E\simeq \operatorname{Rep}(G)\) is completely determined by finite-group data. Since \(\mathcal E=\mathcal E'\) and \(\operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal E)^2=\operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C)\), de-equivariantization produces a pointed fusion category \(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega\) for some \(\omega\in Z^3(G,k^\times)\), and hence
\[
\mathcal C\simeq_{\mathrm{br}} Z(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega)
 \simeq \operatorname{Rep}(D^\omega(G)).
\]
Thus Lagrangian subcategories provide an intrinsic reconstruction of twisted quantum doubles. Applying this criterion to integral nilpotent braided fusion categories yields Lagrangian subcategories in their nondegenerate components and implies that such categories are group-theoretical; in the modular case they are precisely braided representation categories of twisted group doubles. This also reduces their dimensions, simple objects, and modular data to finite nilpotent-group and cohomological information.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you describe the principal theorems connecting prime-power-dimensional modular categories, finite \(p\)-groups, Sylow decomposition, and semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras?
counterfactuals.output:
The relevant results form a categorical analogue of the elementary theory of finite nilpotent groups.

### 1. Prime-power dimension implies categorical nilpotence

Let \(\mathcal C\) be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\). If

\[
\operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C)=p^n
\]

for a prime \(p\), then \(\mathcal C\) is **nilpotent**. Equivalently, it can be built from \(\mathrm{Vec}\) by a sequence of faithful extensions by \(p\)-groups; after refining the series, one may use cyclic groups of order \(p\).

This is the fusion-categorical counterpart of the theorem that every finite \(p\)-group is nilpotent. It implies, among other things, that prime-power-dimensional fusion categories are solvable and possess substantial grading and central structure.

A qualification is important: prime-power global dimension does **not** imply pointedness. For example, Ising categories have dimension \(4\), and Drinfeld centers of nonabelian \(p\)-groups provide integral, nonpointed modular examples.

### 2. The integral case is group-theoretical

If a prime-power-dimensional fusion category is **integral**, meaning that every simple object has integral Frobenius–Perron dimension, then nilpotence gives the stronger conclusion that it is **group-theoretical**.

Thus an integral category of dimension \(p^n\) is categorically controlled by finite \(p\)-group data: pointed categories \(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega\), module categories over them, and their Morita equivalents. This does not mean that every such category is literally \(\operatorname{Rep}(G)\), only that it lies in the Morita-theoretic class generated by twisted \(p\)-group categories.

### 3. Modular categories admit Sylow decomposition

For a braided nilpotent fusion category \(\mathcal C\), there is a canonical prime decomposition

\[
\mathcal C \simeq \boxtimes_{p\mid \operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C)}
\mathcal C_{(p)},
\]

where each \(\mathcal C_{(p)}\) is a braided fusion category of \(p\)-power Frobenius–Perron dimension. These factors are the categorical **Sylow subcategories**.

If \(\mathcal C\) is nondegenerate—hence modular once a compatible ribbon structure is chosen—then every \(\mathcal C_{(p)}\) is nondegenerate as well. Consequently, every nilpotent modular category decomposes uniquely, up to braided equivalence and ordering, into modular prime-power factors.

This is analogous to the unique direct-product decomposition of a finite nilpotent group into its Sylow subgroups. The braided hypothesis is crucial: for a general, nonbraided fusion category, one does not obtain such a canonical tensor-product decomposition.

### 4. Structure specific to prime-power modular categories

A modular category of dimension \(p^n\) is therefore a basic “Sylow block” in the theory of nilpotent modular categories. Such categories have strong restrictions on:

- possible simple-object dimensions;
- the group of invertible objects;
- universal gradings and adjoint subcategories;
- centralizers of fusion subcategories;
- the structure of the associated metric \(p\)-groups in the pointed case.

In the integral case they are group-theoretical. In the nonintegral case, phenomena are concentrated primarily at \(p=2\); Ising-type categories are the standard examples showing why integrality must be stated separately.

### 5. Translation to semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras

If \(H\) is a finite-dimensional semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra, then

\[
\operatorname{FPdim}(\operatorname{Rep} H)=\dim H.
\]

Hence, if \(\dim H=p^n\), the fusion category \(\operatorname{Rep} H\) is nilpotent and solvable. If it is integral—as happens automatically for an actual quasi-Hopf realization with the ordinary vector-space dimension function—then it is group-theoretical.

Conversely, integral fusion categories can be realized as representation categories of finite-dimensional semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras. Thus the categorical prime-power and Sylow theorems yield structural results for semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras even when there is no useful classification of the algebras by generators and relations.

One should distinguish levels of conclusion:

- **categorical equivalence:** \(\operatorname{Rep} H\) is nilpotent or group-theoretical;
- **Morita equivalence:** it is controlled by twisted finite \(p\)-group data;
- **gauge equivalence of algebras:** a stronger statement, not implied in general by group-theoreticality.

If \(\operatorname{Rep} H\) is braided and decomposes into Sylow factors, those factors may be represented by suitable semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras, but this does not generally give a canonical tensor-product decomposition of \(H\) itself.

### Summary

The chain of ideas is

\[
\text{dimension }p^n
\Longrightarrow
\text{nilpotent fusion category}
\]

and, in the integral case,

\[
\text{nilpotent}
\Longrightarrow
\text{group-theoretical}.
\]

For braided or modular nilpotent categories,

\[
\mathcal C \simeq \boxtimes_p \mathcal C_{(p)},
\]

which is the categorical Sylow decomposition. Through representation categories, these theorems transfer to finite-dimensional semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras, with Morita and categorical structure replacing literal decomposition of the underlying algebra.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a journal-style abstract for a paper proving that integral nilpotent braided fusion categories are group-theoretical, with an analogy between Lagrangian subcategories and Manin pairs.
counterfactuals.output: We prove that every integral nilpotent braided fusion category is group-theoretical. The argument combines the upper central series of a nilpotent fusion category with the structure of its Müger center and suitable commutative algebra objects. After passing to the nondegenerate setting via modularization and equivariantization, we construct a Lagrangian fusion subcategory of the Drinfeld center, thereby obtaining a categorical Morita equivalence with a pointed fusion category. This yields the asserted group-theoreticality and gives an intrinsic braided-categorical criterion for its detection. Conceptually, the resulting pair consisting of a nondegenerate braided fusion category and a Lagrangian subcategory is analogous to a Manin pair: the braiding plays the role of a nondegenerate invariant bilinear form, while the Lagrangian subcategory is its maximally isotropic component. This analogy clarifies the role of centers and condensation in the proof and situates nilpotent braided fusion categories within a finite tensor-categorical counterpart of the geometry underlying Lie bialgebras and quantum groups.
